Famous for her passionate love affair with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, Cleopatra VII, one of the few female rulers in ancient Egypt, is often portrayed as a great beauty who knows how to wield charm in pursuit of her ambitions. Lesser known is how the Egyptian empress’ wisdom helped [[1]] her political interests. After all, expanding an empire in a male-dominated world requires more than just physical [[2]].
Nowhere is the queen’s wisdom better reflected than in the way she presented herself in public. The images she chose to [[3]] differed according to her political needs. For example, when crowned at the age of 18, Cleopatra was dressed as Isis, a goddess in ancient Egypt religion, and accompanied by a Buchis, a bull worshiped as a war god. By identifying herself with an ancient goddess and walking alongside with an animal representing male rulers, Cleopatra intended to [[4]] an authentic ruler. Even more brilliantly, despite being a member of the ancient Greek dynasty that took over Egypt in 305 B.C., Cleopatra didn’t choose Greek gods but Egyptian ones. This gesture demonstrated her intention to win [[5]] among the people under her rule. Unlike male rulers’ straightforward aggressiveness, Cleopatra made political advances in a not-so-clear manner.
The empress’ meeting with Mark Antony, one of the rulers of the Roman Empire, is another example of her [[6]] approach. When the Roman general, eager to gain support from Egypt, requested a meeting with Cleopatra, he had the [[7]] idea that the empress had everything planned in advance. Highly aware of what Rome wanted to tap into—Egypt’s immense wealth, Cleopatra made a spectacular [[8]]. She arrived in modern-day Turkey on the fanciest boat Antony had ever seen, decorated with expensive textiles and jewels. Furthermore, the empress had the wit to [[9]] the general’s deep love of Greek culture. Fanned by servants dressed as sea nymphs, Cleopatra, lying under a golden canopy and dressed as Aphrodite, a Greek goddess, succeeded in making the usually [[10]] general fall blindly in love with her.
Cleopatra VII took her own life at the age of 39, which ended her 21-year reign in Egypt. While the world is often fixated on her love life and her beauty, it’s time to acknowledge the young empress’ political sophistication.
